Consult Summary:
- Acute dry, pruritic rash isolated to hands and arms after swimming; dermatitis suspected; treated with emollients, topical steroid, and OTC antihistamines with plan for follow-up if not improving.

History:
- Presenting complaint: Dry, itchy skin on arms and hands.
- Onset/duration: Began a few days ago, after swimming; symptoms have persisted without noted improvement.
- Progression: No documented spreading beyond arms/hands; no systemic symptoms.
- Exposures/triggers: Recent swimming (possible irritant exposure); used coconut butter without relief; weather/stress noted as potential contributing factors.
- Associated symptoms: Skin red and dry; no cracking mentioned; no fever, vomiting, or body-wide symptoms.
- Alleviating/ aggravating factors: Emollients (coconut butter) did not help; unknown effect of swimming on symptoms beyond initial onset.
- Review of systems: No fever, no GI symptoms, no urinary issues; appetite and energy reported as generally ok aside from fatigue.
- Other: Feels stressed at work (teacher); no new soaps/cleansers reported; no known skin problems previously.
- Sensitivities/allergies: Lactose intolerance noted.
- Medications: Microgynon (contraceptive pill) reported; dose/route/frequency not documented.
- Social history: Lives alone; non-smoker; does not drink alcohol; works as a primary school teacher; single exposure at work noted as potential stress contributor.
- Family history: Father with asthma; mother with hayfever.

Past Medical History:
- No chronic conditions documented.
- No prior history of eczema or dermatitis reported.

Medications:
- Microgynon (dose/route/frequency not documented).

Allergies:
- Lactose intolerance noted.

Social History:
- Lives alone; non-smoker; no alcohol use; works as a primary school teacher; high work-related stress.

Family History:
- Father: asthma; Mother: hayfever.

Physical Examination:
- Vitals: Not recorded.
- Exam findings: Not recorded in formal skin exam; patient reports a dry, red, itchy rash on hands and arms. No widespread spread reported; no fever or systemic signs described.
- Additional observations: Not documented.

Investigations:
- None ordered or reported.

Assessment & Plan:
- Overall Impression:
  - Working diagnosis: Dermatitis of the hands/arms, likely irritant contact dermatitis with possible contributions from allergic contact dermatitis or atopic dermatitis.
- DDx Integration (brief):
  - Irritant contact dermatitis
    - Supporting: Onset after swimming; rash confined to exposed areas (hands/arms); dry, red, itchy skin; no systemic symptoms.
    - Opposing: Specific culprit exposures (pool chemicals, soaps, etc.) not identified.
  - Allergic contact dermatitis
    - Supporting: Potential exposures (pool chemicals, coconut butter, soaps); pruritic erythematous rash.
    - Opposing: No confirmed allergen or clear temporal relationship beyond swimming.
  - Atopic dermatitis
    - Supporting: Dry, itchy skin; family history of atopy (father with asthma, mother with hayfever).
    - Opposing: No personal history of eczema; acute onset over a few days.
- Issue 1: Dermatitis (acute, localized to hands/arms)
  - Plan:
    - Topical corticosteroid cream to affected areas (dose/route/frequency not documented).
    - Emollient applied routinely (throughout the day for the next few days).
    - OTC antihistamines for itch (e.g., Piriton or Loratadine); dose/route/frequency not documented.
    - Avoid potential triggers (e.g., swimming exposure, irritants; continue monitoring).
    - Patient information leaflet on dermatitis provided.
    - Analgesia not recommended as helpful in this scenario; Paracetamol specifically noted as not helpful.
    - Follow-up in 1 week or sooner if symptoms worsen or do not improve.
- Issue 2: Medication reconciliation and safety
  - Plan:
    - Continue Microgynon as previously prescribed; no changes documented here (dose/route/frequency not documented).
    - Review lactose intolerance status as part of allergy history; no dietary modifications currently advised.
- Issue 3: Counseling and safety netting
  - Plan:
    - Educate on when to return (worsening spread, fever, lesions, signs of infection).
    - Return if no improvement after 1 week for re-evaluation.

General plan:
- Continue currently offered dermatitis treatments; reassess in 1 week.
- Consider escalation to stronger topical steroids or patch testing if symptoms persist or worsen.

Quality checks:
- Missing but clinically expected elements: Vitals not provided; formal skin examination details not documented.
- Conflicts between transcript and DDx: None detected; no explicit conflict noted.
- Transcript quality: Sufficient to establish symptoms and management plan; minor gaps in exam documentation.

Document quality notes:
- Allergies documented (lactose intolerance) but not clearly listed as medication allergy; considered as allergy history per transcript.
- Med reconciliation: One medication (Microgynon) without dose/route/frequency.
- No labs or imaging ordered.
